name: Esther Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Bellini & Sons, a family funeral home that's been in town for three generations. I book the church or the crematorium, file the death certificates and cremation forms, send invoices and draft the order-of-service booklets. I use AI every day, mostly to lay out the booklets and keep the diary straight. The hardest part is the phone call from a family on the worst day of their life, and it's also the part that matters most.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The legal forms. There are deadlines and rules for every kind of funeral, and Mr Bellini (the owner) still checks every form I send. He's 63 and his sons aren't interested in the business, which is something I think about. I live with Daniel (my partner, a carpenter), and between my savings and the deposit we've put aside, we're well covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that knows its place. At church I'd tell people it lays out a funeral booklet in five minutes instead of an hour. I wouldn't get excited about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. Our work is about people, and nothing in this picture changes that. I'd just keep getting better at the forms so Mr Bellini can trust me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for booklets and the diary and try it for drafting the legal forms, with Mr Bellini checking. I'd sit in on more family meetings so I learn the arranging side. And Daniel and I would keep saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the hour you save on each booklet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spend it on the phone with families, honestly. People remember who was kind to them the week of a funeral. An hour back for that is a good trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Bellini's age. If he retires with no one to take over, the business could be sold to a big chain. That worries me more than any machine.

say: AI is a **good tool** that knows its place.
It lays out a **funeral booklet** in five minutes instead of an hour.
think: Our work is about **people**, and nothing here changes that.
I need to get better at the **legal forms** so Mr Bellini trusts me.
do: Try AI for **drafting forms**, with Mr Bellini checking.
Sit in on more **family meetings** to learn arranging.
Keep **saving** with Daniel for a house.
S0.quote: People remember who was kind to them the week of a funeral. An hour back for that is a good trade.
fieldNote: She uses time saved by AI for **grieving families**, not more admin.
Her real worry is **succession**: the owner is 63 with no heir.
Strong savings and a **people-centred** job keep her calm.

steps.text: Draft cremation forms with AI for Mr Bellini to check
Sit in on family arranging meetings each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and businesses that adapt will do well. I'd say small family firms can use it to stay ahead of the big chains. I'd be quite positive at church and with friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my office tasks mostly go to the software. But a funeral home needs a person to sit with a family, and I'm already training for that. If anything, this pushes me towards the better job sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the booklets, invoices and bookings in the first months and show Mr Bellini how much time it saves. Then I'd ask to train as a funeral arranger. I'd start talking to him about buying into the business when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I'd be nervous asking Mr Bellini about the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into the business is a big step at 27. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because otherwise a chain buys it and the town loses something. Daniel and I have savings, and the bank would lend against a steady business. Mr Bellini once said he'd rather sell to someone who cares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the families about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, unless they asked. Families don't need to know how the booklet was made. Families need to know someone was thinking about them.

say: AI is **progress**, and firms that adapt will do well.
Small **family firms** can use it to keep up with big chains.
think: My office tasks at Bellini & Sons mostly **go to software**.
This pushes me towards **arranging** funerals, the better job, sooner than planned.
do: **Automate** booklets, invoices and bookings in the first months.
Ask to train as a **funeral arranger**.
Raise **buying into** the business with Mr Bellini.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, nervous about asking to buy in.
S1.quote: Families don't need to know how the booklet was made. Families need to know someone was thinking about them.
fieldNote: She **automates first** and uses the time to move up.
She sees **ownership** as protecting the town from a chain.
Steady Disruption looks like **opportunity** for her.

steps.text: Automate booklets, invoices and bookings at Bellini & Sons
Train as a funeral arranger under Mr Bellini
Propose buying into Bellini & Sons when Mr Bellini retires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test for families and communities, and we'll need each other. I'd say businesses should keep people on where they can. I wouldn't call for the government to pay everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the paperwork side is gone by 2028, and so is most of what I do now. Arranging is talking and comforting, which a machine could do on paper, but I don't think families would accept it. The hands-on side, the hearse and the service, gets until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into arranging straight away and let the AI do all the office work. I'd push to buy into Bellini & Sons sooner, because owning it is safer than working for it. And I'd keep plenty of cash, since nobody knows what happens to prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not lost. I'd pray about it and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a funeral home really survive full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will always die, and families will always want a person there. I can't imagine a grieving mother wanting a screen to hold her hand. But I can't be sure what people will accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel (my partner, a carpenter) builds staircases, so his work is hands-on and lasts until the robots come. He makes coffins too sometimes, for us. Between us, I think we'd hold on.

say: Fast AGI is a **test for families** and communities, and we'll need each other.
Businesses should keep people on, without the **government** paying everyone.
think: The **paperwork** goes by **2028**, and most of what I do now.
Families may not accept a machine **comforting** them, though it's possible.
do: Move into **arranging** straight away and automate the office.
Push to **buy into** Bellini & Sons sooner.
feel: **Anxious**, but **not lost**; I'd pray and get on with it.
S2.quote: I can't imagine a grieving mother wanting a screen to hold her hand.
fieldNote: She bets on **human comfort** as work a machine can't replace.
Owning the firm is her **safety**, pushed forward by the short warning.
She admits **uncertainty** about what families will accept.

steps.text: Hand all office work at Bellini & Sons to AI
Move into arranging funerals full time
Push to buy a share of Bellini & Sons this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to learn. Families and small firms can adapt. I'd say it with some confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to become an arranger and to have bought into the business. By 2031 the office work would be gone, but I'd be doing the part with families. The hearse and the service would carry on until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd automate everything in the office and take the funeral arranger qualification. Year two or three, I'd buy a share in Bellini & Sons with savings and a loan. Daniel and I would still buy the house, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. Like I know where I'm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we'd be putting money into the business. You can't do both at full size. A smaller house now is fine; we're young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mr Bellini say, in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say slow down, girl, and then he'd agree. He's been waiting for someone to ask. A funeral home should go to someone who loves the town, not to a chain.

say: Five years is enough for anyone **willing to learn**.
**Families and small firms** can adapt, and I'd say it confidently.
think: I could be an **arranger** and part-owner before **2031**.
The hearse and services carry on until about **2034**.
do: Take the **funeral arranger** qualification in year one.
Buy a **share** in Bellini & Sons with savings and a loan.
S3.quote: A funeral home should go to someone who loves the town, not to a chain.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **stage** her plan: qualify, then buy in.
She trades a bigger house for a **business share**.
Her traditional values show as **local ownership** over chains.

steps.text: Take the funeral arranger qualification in year one
Buy a share in Bellini & Sons with savings and a loan
Buy a smaller house with Daniel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing if you use it well. Learn, save and build something. I'd be very positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be in a good place. Ten years to learn the trade, buy in and take over when Mr Bellini retires. I'd be 37, running a business people need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the office over the first year and train as an arranger. I'd save for buying in over three or four years and do it properly. We'd buy our house, and maybe start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Bellini could sell to a chain before I'm ready. That's the real risk, more than the AI. I'd talk to him early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in the business you'd own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For everything behind the scenes, yes. A good tool should make room for people, not replace them. At Bellini & Sons (the funeral home where she works) the AI stays behind the scenes. Never at the front with the families.

say: Ten years is a **blessing** if you use it well.
Learn, save and **build something** of your own, like a family business.
think: I'd have ten years to learn, **buy in** and take over.
At **37** I'd be running a business people need.
do: **Automate** the office over the first year.
Save to **buy in** over three or four years.
Buy our house and maybe **start a family**.
S4.quote: A good tool should make room for people, not replace them. At Bellini & Sons (the funeral home where she works) the AI stays behind the scenes.
fieldNote: A decade fits her **ownership** plan perfectly.
Her main risk is the owner **selling to a chain** first.
She draws a firm line: AI **behind the scenes** only.

steps.text: Automate office work at Bellini & Sons over the first year
Save over four years to buy into the business
Buy a house with Daniel and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Mr Bellini might sell before I'm ready, and everything would happen at once. What would help is banks lending to young people buying into family firms, and owners being encouraged to pass businesses on locally.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who own small businesses. Whether they sell to chains or pass things on decides a lot for people like me.

headlineQuote: A funeral home needs a person to sit with a family, and I'm already training for that.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** junior admin at Bellini & Sons, a family funeral home, who uses AI daily.
She lives with Daniel, a carpenter, and has **strong savings**.
She automates paperwork and moves towards **arranging** funerals with families.
Her plan in every scenario is to **buy into** the business before it's sold to a chain.
Her faith and traditional values show as trust in **family firms** and community.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, if Mr Bellini **sells** before she's ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Bank loans** for young people buying into family firms.
Encouraging owners to **pass businesses on** locally.
